title: Abuse and the churches
hook: abuse and its cover-up in churches of more than one tradition have caused deep harm; survivors deserve belief and justice

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rwanda, clothes on the benches of a church kept as a memorial. Your line was never again, truly. Did you refuse to laugh along? Day nine hundred seventy-four.

Before anything else: today's lesson is about abuse in churches. If it touches your own story, you can stop here, and nothing is lost. A grown man sits in a church office across from an official. Slowly, he tells what a trusted leader did to him when he was a boy. The official listens, nods, writes something down, and thanks him for coming. Then nothing happens. The leader is quietly moved somewhere else, where nobody knows. Today, a wound inside the churches themselves, and what the Bible says to those who caused it.

Journalists, courts, survivors and church inquiries have uncovered the abuse of children and vulnerable adults by priests, pastors, youth leaders and volunteers. It has been found in Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Protestant and evangelical churches. This is not one church's story. And survivors describe a second harm on top of the first: the cover-up. Leaders who moved abusers to new places. Families pressed to keep quiet for the sake of the church's name. Children who told and weren't believed. The Bible is not quiet about this. Jesus sets a child in the middle of his disciples and says, in the King James Bible: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea." In the King James English, to offend someone is to make them stumble. Long before, the prophet Ezekiel had turned on leaders who look after themselves instead of the flock: "Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?" And Jesus warns that hiding doesn't last: "For nothing is secret, that shall not be made manifest." Forgiveness has sometimes been used as a weapon here, survivors pushed to forgive and stay silent. But survivors and their advocates insist that forgiving is not the same as hiding, and it does not replace justice. Churches in many countries now have safeguarding rules, apologies, and in some places payments to survivors. Survivors who have spoken out say what they need is simpler: to be believed, for the truth to be told, and for it to stop.

Here's the practice: hold survivors with care. Settle, and breathe. If this is your story, simply breathe, and know you can talk to someone you trust or a support line whenever you choose. If it isn't, bring to mind survivors of abuse, in churches and anywhere else. Don't picture what happened. Picture them now: getting through a day, telling someone, being listened to. If you pray, you can pray for survivors, and for leaders to tell the truth. If you don't, stay with them in silence for a while. The bell holds the time.
Millstone. The weight Jesus says belongs around the neck of anyone who harms a child, a warning answered first by believing survivors.
Your line: believe them. Today, if someone tells you something hard about what was done to them, listen all the way through before you say a word. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Churches across traditions have adopted safeguarding policies, background checks for anyone working with children, and named people to whom abuse can be reported, alongside reporting to the police. Some hold services of lament and apology with survivors.

fork.setup: you're a church leader. a young person tells you a trusted volunteer hurt them. what do you do?
options: move the volunteer quietly to another church.
believe them, protect them, and report it.
ask them to forgive and keep it private.
fork.reveal: survivors ask first to be believed, and safeguarding rules now say report it. moving abusers on was the cover-up.

original.note: Greek: should cause to stumble, the word the King James Bible renders offend (Matthew 18:6).

trapdoor: what you thought: a scandal in one church you read about once.
what it means: abuse in churches across traditions, made worse by cover-up, where survivors ask to be believed.
what a scholar hears: skandalizō, to trip someone up. in Matthew 18:6 Jesus attaches a millstone to it.

notes: Sensitive day. A content note opens the hook and the practice offers survivors a way out; consider whether the app should also show a support resource (no phone numbers written into the script, since they vary by country).
Claims rule: no counts or statistics. 'Survivors describe a second harm' is drawn from inquiries; confirm.
The hook scene is composed, not a specific case.
'Offend there means to trip someone up, to make them fall' glosses skandalizō; standard lexical sense; confirm.
Ezekiel 34 is aimed at Israel's rulers; it is applied here to religious leaders, which some readers may question. Confirm.
howItsDone: safeguarding described generally; confirm. 'Services of lament and apology' described generally.
Original: σκανδαλίσῃ (aorist subjunctive, Matthew 18:6); confirm form and pronunciation.

Editor pass: Ezekiel 34 described as aimed at 'leaders who look after themselves' (matching 'feed themselves') rather than 'religious leaders who protect themselves'; the skandalizo gloss now describes the KJV word 'offend'; the forgiveness line and 'what matters most' are attributed to survivors rather than stated by the narrator; varied a practice line repeated across nearby days.
Editor pass 2: the forgiveness myth answer is now attributed to survivors and advocates, as in the teach, instead of stated by the narrator.

Audit (fresh): 'No tradition gets to point at another' (teach and myth reveal) read as the narrator moralizing; now 'This is not one church's story'. 'Churches now have safeguarding rules' was sweeping; now 'Churches in many countries'.
